name: Nanofat / autologous fat grafting

lead: Fat transfer moves a person's own fat to another area. Nanofat is an emulsified, filtered form used for scars and skin texture.
Published studies are mostly small series and uncontrolled reports.

paras: Liposuctioned fat is processed and reinjected; for nanofat, the liquid contains stromal vascular cells proposed to aid tissue repair.
Reported effects include swelling, bruising, donor-site pain, infection, contour irregularities and fat necrosis.

lead: Fat transfer, also called fat grafting or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat, usually harvested by liposuction, to another area to correct volume loss or irregularities.[1] Nanofat is a variant in which fat is mechanically emulsified and filtered into a liquid injected through very fine needles, used for scars and skin quality rather than volume.[2][3]

Studies on scars and skin quality are mostly small clinical series, and a 2019 review describes nanofat and related adipose-derived products as having shown capability to repair and rejuvenate tissue.[4] Wikipedia notes that much of the fat-transfer article's sourcing comes from clinic websites rather than peer-reviewed studies.[1]

paras: Fat grafting has three stages: harvesting, processing and reinjection.[1] In the 2013 description of nanofat, microfat is processed into a fine emulsion injected with needles up to 27 gauge for superficial defects.[2] Wikipedia says nanografts contain no intact adipose cells but retain stem-cell content.[1]

The original 2013 report described nanofat grafting in 67 cases for superficial problems and presented preliminary cell-content findings.[2] A 2018 clinic analysis studied nanofat on scars, wrinkles and discolorations.[3] A 2017 study compared modified nanofat procedures with the classic method in scars, relating results to stromal vascular fraction yield.[5] Other published work covers condensed nanofat combined with fat grafts for atrophic scars, unfiltered nanofat for post-burn facial scars, and facial rejuvenation with nanofat.[6][7][8] Registered trials include post-burn facial scars (48 participants), atrophic scars (20), nanofat with microneedling in scars (30), and infraorbital rejuvenation (60).[9][10][11][12] The sources reviewed here do not give controlled effect sizes.

For fat grafting generally, Wikipedia lists swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, infection, contour irregularities and fat necrosis; it says up to 50% of transferred fat may be reabsorbed in breast augmentation.[1]

timeline.event: Nanofat grafting described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[2]
